The Grand Mosque seizure was the armed takeover of the Great Mosque of Mecca, the holiest site in Islam, from 20 November to 4 December 1979. Several hundred militants led by Juhayman al-Otaybi held it for two weeks.

Juhayman, a former National Guard soldier, accused the Saudi royal family of corruption and of selling out Islam to the West. At dawn prayers on the first day of the year 1400 in the Islamic calendar, his men took the mosque and declared his brother-in-law to be the Mahdi, the redeemer expected at the end of time.

Saudi forces needed a religious ruling to fight inside the sanctuary, and the battle through the mosque and its cellars was long and bloody, with French advisers helping. Hundreds died, including pilgrims; the leaders who survived were executed.

The kingdom answered by giving its clerics more power. Rules on women tightened, and money flowed to spread conservative teaching abroad. This lasted until the reforms of the 2010s that let women drive. It came in the same year as the Iranian Revolution, which also challenged Saudi Arabia.
